new_statements.quote: El yuki presenta generalmente el acento en la penúltima sílaba. Pero en la acentuación de un lexema yuki se tiene en cuenta la cantidad silábica como también la existencia o no de diptongos. [2.4.1] El acento de una raíz o lexema bisilábico es siempre grave, ocurre en la penúltima sílaba. ... Una excepción es cuando la última sílaba contiene los diptongos -ai, -oi, -ui en este caso, este lleva el acento. ... [2.4.2] El comportamiento de los lexemas trisilábicos es variado ... [2.4.3] Los lexemas tetrasilábicos llevan un acento grave en la penúltima sílaba. [2.4.4] Lexemas pentasilábicos o con cinco sílabas, llevan acento en la penúltima sílaba.
new_statements.translation: Yuki generally has the stress on the penultimate syllable. But in stressing a Yuki lexeme, the number of syllables is taken into account, as well as the presence or absence of diphthongs. [2.4.1] The stress of a disyllabic root or lexeme is always paroxytone, it falls on the penultimate syllable. ... An exception is when the last syllable contains the diphthongs -ai, -oi, -ui; in this case that syllable carries the stress. ... [2.4.2] The behaviour of trisyllabic lexemes is varied ... [2.4.3] Tetrasyllabic lexemes carry paroxytone stress on the penultimate syllable. [2.4.4] Pentasyllabic lexemes carry stress on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is penultimate (Yuki is grouped with the penult-stressing Tupi-Guarani languages, against PTG final stress). Disyllables, tetrasyllables, pentasyllables and hexasyllables (prefixes counted) are stressed on the penult. A final syllable with a falling diphthong -ai/-oi/-ui takes the stress instead. Trisyllabic lexemes are lexically variable (penult or antepenult, or final), with syllables containing kwa/gwa/kya/kyo or -ai/-oi attracting stress; because of this irregularity trisyllables are written with an accent mark in the vocabulary. Monosyllabic roots with a prefix stress the prefix (behaving as a disyllable). Some suffixes attract stress; a disyllabic suffix string takes penult stress itself.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; 'acento primario' is mentioned only for prefix+disyllabic-root forms (prefix bears primary stress, p. 28). No secondary-stress rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Final diphthongs -ai/-oi/-ui attract stress (isái 'rocío', ixói 'lluvia'); trisyllables vary between penult (baráso 'gusano') and antepenult (yéreta 'perro') and final (barakwá 'enseñar', gurekyó 'tener'), with kwa/gwa/kya/kyo and -ai/-oi syllables attracting stress; pentasyllables ending in -kya stress the final low vowel (abanurukyá 'silla'); certain suffixes (e.g. -ta, -niá) attract stress off the root.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated over the lexeme/root by syllable count, with prefixes and suffixes counted into the word (2.4.6 'Lexemas + sufijos'); citation forms. Phrase level: declarative intonation falls from the last stressed syllable (2.6.1, p. 30).
new_statements.identity_note: Villafañe 2004 describes 'yuki' as spoken at Bia Recuaté (Chimoré region, Cochabamba, Bolivia) = Glottolog yuqu1240 Yuqui (ISO yuq); no dialect split. Note Glottolog's ref list for yuqu1240 wrongly includes dos Anjos 2005 'Fonologia Katukina (Dialeto Katukina do Biá)', which is a Katukinan language of Brazil, not Yuqui — ignore it.
